extracted.intended_audience: poets, rhetoricians, literary critics, and writers interested in the mechanics of poetic/rhetorical effect
extracted.subtask_description: Principled guidance for composing and judging poetry and eloquence focused on how words produce effects (sound, image, and passion), the proper balance of clarity and force, and avoiding common faults such as bombast or needless pictorial detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words affect by sound and habit rather than by picturing
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound-abstract words (virtue, honor, persuasion, etc.) do not derive their power from raising precise mental images; they operate chiefly by their sound and by habitual association with occasions in which they were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abstract, conventionally-charged words to evoke feeling even when no clear image is conjured. Example: many are moved by the words 'virtue' or 'honour' though they cannot form a precise idea of the particular actions signified. Anti-pattern: expecting every abstract term to carry a clear, composite idea; over-analysing such words can dissipate their force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and choose word-types appropriately (aggregate / simple abstract / compound abstract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words divide into aggregates (man, tree), simple abstracts (red, round), and compound abstracts (virtue, justice); each class has different capacities for producing sound, picture, and affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you want sensory imagery favor aggregate and simple-abstract words; when you want moral/sentimental force, compound abstracts (by habitual application) may be more effective. Example guidance from text: compound abstracts produce sound and affection but rarely a picture; aggregate words are more likely to produce pictures when an effort of imagination is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that general words taught before particulars condition feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Most general moral terms (virtue, vice, good, evil) are learned before specific instances and thereby implant the love/abhorrence associated with them, sometimes producing a mismatch between professed principles and particular actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or writing for impressionable audiences, recognise that applying abstract moral terms early can implant durable feelings. Anti-pattern: using general laudatory words without aligning them to concrete occasions, which can cause confusion of ideas and affections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast; ensure propriety and application of affecting words
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting together highly affecting words without rational application, or in combinations that do not properly agree, creates 'bombast' and undermines sense and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against merely piling impressive words; seek propriety and logical/affective fit. Example anti-pattern: a string of grand terms with no connection to specifics ('wise, valiant, generous, good, and great') used without occasion becomes unoperative or ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the three effects of words: sound, picture, and affection
rubrics_metrics.description: Words can produce (1) the sound, (2) a picture or representation of the thing signified, and (3) an affection (emotion) — different words and constructions favor different effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with awareness of which effect you want to produce. Compound abstracts mainly produce sound and affection; simple abstracts and aggregates can produce pictures as well. Practical note: in ordinary rapid discourse pictures are rarely formed; aim for sound/affection when quick impact is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize strength (passionate force) versus clarity according to purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear expression (concerned with the understanding) and strong expression (concerned with the passions) are distinct; a language or style praised for perspicuity may lack force, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your goal is to instruct (favor clarity) or to move (favor strength). Example: polished, clear languages may be deficient in strength; rougher idioms often convey more passion. Anti-pattern: conflating clarity with strength and expecting one to guarantee the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey speakerly passion and sympathy to move the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Words convey not only subject matter but also the manner in which the speaker is affected; sympathy lets hearers take part in others' passions, and well-chosen verbal tokens can fully express those circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dispositions of words (tone, rhythm, heated diction) that mark strong feeling; in performance, impassioned delivery (tone, countenance, gesture) amplifies verbal effect. Example: impassioned diction can make a description effective even without vivid imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit combinatory power of language to create sublime effects
rubrics_metrics.description: By combining words and adding circumstances in ways unavailable to other arts (painting, sculpture), language can give fresh life and force to simple objects and raise the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strategic concatenation and juxtaposition to produce effects only language can: e.g., 'angel of the Lord', 'shades of Death', 'a universe of death.' These linguistic additions can intensify the sublime beyond what mere pictorial depiction accomplishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry operates chiefly by substitution and sympathy, not strict imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive poetry functions by substitution — sounds that by custom stand for realities and their effects — and by showing effects upon minds (sympathy), rather than by resembling objects exactly as in pictorial imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing descriptive poetry emphasize the feelings elicited and the mental effects, rather than attempting photographic imitation. Note: dramatic poetry (animi motus effert interprete lingua) is closer to strict imitation since it represents manners and passions directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less pictorial detail can increase poetic energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry need not, and often should not, raise full sensible images; insisting on vivid pictorial detail can weaken the force and propriety of poetic diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider using general, elevated mention instead of minute description to heighten effect (examples: lines about Helen, Virgil's passages). Anti-pattern: long, elaborate pictorial descriptions that dissipate the emotional or sublime force of a passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge a work by how well it answers its intended end (proportion and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: As in architecture, rules of proportion determine praise or censure according to whether the work fulfils the end for which it was designed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess compositional choices against the intended aim — if the end is to move, clarity that undermines feeling is blameworthy; if the end is instruction, obscurity for the sake of force is blameworthy. Use the 'end-fulfilled' standard when evaluating arts generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage conventional application and occasion to imbue words with power
rubrics_metrics.description: Words acquire force by repeated application in particular affecting occasions; even after severing the original connection to particulars, the sound continues to operate with similar effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciously deploy words that have established associations through cultural or habitual use to trigger emotion. Caution: overuse or loss of referential grounding can make words mere sounds—still operative, but potentially hollow if not handled with care.
